title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
hook: the gods at the end of their strength, a fire, and a goddess who rises out of it with work to do

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama opened its first window: Sri Mata, the Mother, before Queen and lion throne. Whose favorite name did you use? Today, the next two names, and a fire. Day one thousand one hundred one.

The gods have run out of answers. A demon has the upper hand, and nothing they've tried has worked. So, in the story told around this hymn, they build a great fire and begin a sacrifice. They pour in offerings, and then, when the offerings aren't enough, tradition says they begin to offer themselves. The fire roars higher. And out of it, out of the flames, a goddess rises: radiant, calm, and already knowing what she's come to do. That is Lalita's arrival. Today, the two names that hold that moment.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE RUN OUT OF ANSWERS.` → `A FIRE, AND A SACRIFICE.` → `OUT OF THE FLAMES, A GODDESS.`

segments.voice: Here are the names, in paraphrase. The fourth: she who was born from the fire-altar of consciousness. The fifth: she who rose up, ready for the work of the gods. Start with the fire. In the story, it's a real sacrifice, an altar with flames. But the name doesn't say a fire of wood. It says a fire of consciousness: chit, awareness itself. So the hymn quietly turns the story inward. Commentators have read that in more than one way. Some say the goddess is born wherever awareness burns clear and steady, so the fire-altar is also the heart of the one who sits and recites. Others keep the story's sense in front: the gods' sacrifice was so total that only something made of pure consciousness could answer it. Either way, notice where she isn't born. Not from a womb, not from a bargain. From a fire. Then the second name, and it's practical. She rose up ready for the work of the gods. She doesn't arrive to be admired. She arrives with a task. The gods had a problem they couldn't solve, and she comes up out of the flames already turned toward the work. Put the two names side by side and you get a small portrait of how this tradition pictures the goddess. Pure awareness, and a job to do. Inner fire, and outer work. Some readers take comfort in that: deep stillness and practical help are not two different goddesses. They're one, rising out of one fire. Tomorrow the hymn turns to what she holds in her hands.
screen: `BORN FROM THE FIRE-ALTAR.` · `A FIRE MADE OF CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `NOT FROM A WOMB. FROM A FIRE.` · `READY FOR THE WORK OF THE GODS.` · then, large: `INNER FIRE, OUTER WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: aware, then ready. Settle, and let the breath slow. For the first part of the sit, don't do anything with the mind. Just notice that you're aware: sounds arrive, the breath moves, a thought passes, and something is knowing all of it. Rest in that knowing. When the mind wanders, notice that too, and come back. Then, before the bell, let one plain question rise out of the stillness: what work is mine today? Don't force an answer. Let it come up the way the name says she rose, ready. If you pray, you can offer the question to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. If you don't, just let it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn whose fourth and fifth names say she was born from the fire of consciousness, and rose ready for the work of the gods.
Your line: the Lalita Sahasranama, selections. Today, pick one task that's truly yours and begin it from a still place, not a rushed one. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Lalita Sahasranama before a lamp or a sacred fire, and in Sri Vidya worship the recitation is sometimes joined to fire offerings.

original.note: Sanskrit: cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā, 'born from the fire-altar of consciousness,' the fourth name in the Lalita Sahasranama.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess born from a fire is a fairy-tale image.
what it means: the name says the fire was consciousness itself, and the next name says she rose with work to do.
what a scholar hears: cit-agni-kuṇḍa-sambhūtā, devakārya-samudyatā: the Lalitopakhyana's sacrifice story, read by commentators as awareness giving birth to the goddess.

notes: Names 4–5 paraphrased: cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā, devakāryasamudyatā. Calling them 'the fourth' and 'the fifth' follows the standard numbering after śrīmātā, śrīmahārājñī, śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī; confirm.

The sacrifice story (gods losing to the demon Bhandasura, holding a sacrifice and offering themselves into the fire, Lalita emerging) is from the Lalitopakhyana; told as 'the story told around this hymn' and 'tradition says'. The demon is not named aloud. Confirm the outline.
Two commentarial readings of the fire of consciousness given without ranking; confirm they are fair (cf. Bhaskararaya's Saubhagya Bhaskara).
Day 1102 (already written) opens 'after names that tell of her rising from a fire of consciousness' and turns to her hands; this day's close points there.
